title: More, longer, more diverse realistic fluid sims (with color mixing)
objective: Follow-up to improve-basic-fluid-sim-realism, whose renders looked close to the photoreal target but were very short and limited. Produce a diverse, extensive, and much longer set of realistic fluid animations that show off the same pipeline: several distinct starting conditions, two viscosities (thin water and thick honey), and at least one color-mixing scene where two differently colored liquids swirl together and blend. The improved renderer in sim/fluid_render2.py is reused verbatim by importing it (its filled-interior mask, distance-transform thickness, Beer-Lambert depth color, refraction/Fresnel/specular, foam); all new drivers, scenes, the faucet emitter, the Newtonian viscosity term, and the per-particle color advection live in a fresh module sim/fluid_showcase_render.py, and the shared files sim/fluid_render2.py, sim/fluid_viscosity.py, sim/material_showcase.py were left untouched. Visual quality and duration are the graded axes; this makes no claim of physical light transport, real-time performance, or differentiability.
findings: PARTIAL / INTERIM: the render worker was interrupted after 3 of the planned scenes (pour, fill, obstacle) were rendered; color-mixing, honey, and dam-break were not reached. This manifest was reconciled to reference only the media that exists. A faster re-run will regenerate the full set.
hypothesis: The duration result is a direct consequence of where a weakly-compressible MPM fluid puts its energy and how the scheme removes it. The only restoring stress is a pressure on the volume ratio J, which does no work once the fluid is level, so a released body converts potential energy into a single splash and then has nothing to sustain motion; meanwhile the APIC transfers and any explicit viscosity are dissipative, so the kinetic energy decays roughly exponentially and the surface goes quiet in about a second regardless of how stiff or how lightly damped the fluid is. Sustained motion therefore has to be supplied from outside the closed energy budget, either by continuously injecting new fluid with kinetic energy (the faucet) or by choosing a material whose own sluggishness stretches the motion over the clip (the thick honey, whose large viscosity makes even a slow pour take seconds to relax). The color result rests on the particle carrying identity: a Lagrangian tracer that the dynamics move but never read is advected with zero numerical diffusion, so the blend seen at the interface is not the dye diffusing but the two sharply-colored populations becoming spatially interleaved by the resolved flow, with the renderer's local average reading that interleaving as an intermediate hue. The blur width that forms the local average is the knob that decides whether the mix reads at all: too narrow gives a speckled seam, too wide washes the whole body to a muddy uniform tone, and a width matched to the density blur gives a legible band a few particle-spacings wide. What would test the generality of these claims beyond this set: whether the faucet trick sustains motion at other resolutions and box geometries, whether the same passive-tracer compositing holds up for more than two colors or for a genuinely 3D view, and whether a real diffusion term added to the dye (rather than pure advection) would produce a more physically faithful concentration field. The scope here is a fixed 2D grid (n_grid = 128), f32, one parameter set per scene.
limitations: Still a stylized 2D side-view render graded on how it looks, not a physical light-transport simulation, and reusing the prior pass's honest caveats: the thickness driving absorption and refraction is a screen-space distance transform of a 2D mask rather than a real optical path through a 3D volume, the caustics are painted, and every color and coefficient is chosen by eye. The dye is a PASSIVE color advection, not a model of how real liquids mix: there is no molecular diffusion and no reaction, so a red particle never becomes purple, and the visible blend is purely two interleaved populations plus the renderer averaging their colors over a hand-tuned blur width. At infinite resolution the blend would resolve back into interleaved red and blue rather than a true continuum of concentration. The labels water and honey are evocative, not calibrated: the mapping from mu_visc to a physical viscosity is not measured, only the thin-versus-thick ordering is honest, and the honey timestep is hand-tuned to the explicit-diffusion stability edge rather than solved implicitly, so honey here is thick-but-finite. The faucet emitter grows the active particle count over time and continually adds mass, so the tank fill level and the exact splash shapes depend on the emission rate, inlet geometry, and box size, all chosen by eye; the thin falling stream is roughly one particle wide and the metaball reconstruction breaks it into droplets and reads it partly as white spray, which is why the colored streams show their hue mainly once they pool. A small FLIP admixture (0.05-0.07) is used to keep splashes lively; it injects energy, so it is kept low enough that viscosity and the boundaries still let each scene settle over a long rollout rather than drifting up, and finiteness plus late frames were checked, but GPU atomic-add accumulation is not bitwise reproducible so exact splash geometry drifts run to run. No gradients, loss, or optimization are involved anywhere; the renderer and these scenes are deliberately non-differentiable and offline.

results.caption: A steady faucet pours a stream of water onto a shallow pool for twelve seconds. The stream plunges and throws a continuous crown, and the pool rises and sloshes under it. Motion is sustained for the whole clip because the faucet keeps feeding fresh fluid, where a single released blob would have gone flat in about a second. The body is a clean depth-graded translucent volume with a bent studio background and torn white spray at the impact.
Hero still from the pour scene.

A faucet fills an initially near-empty tank over about thirteen seconds, the brief's filling condition. The rising surface keeps sloshing under the plunging stream and climbs steadily toward the brim, the water darkening from pale shallow edge to deep interior as it deepens. A continuous-forcing scene: the stream sustains the splashing for the whole clip.
Hero still from the fill scene.

A faucet jet strikes a fixed circular pillar in the tank and forks left and right around it for twelve seconds. The pillar reads as a clean dark disk the water flows around, and because the stream keeps feeding the fork it stays active the whole clip. The obstacle is a slip boundary applied on the grid: velocity into the disk is removed and particles that drift inside are pushed back to its surface.
Hero still from the obstacle scene.
